opus-5.5.text:
I think the most essential difference is **reasoning**. Traditional AI agents, whether a robot in a lab or a reinforcement learning agent playing Atari or Go, are mostly about mapping observations to actions. You see the screen and decide to move left or right. The action space is defined by the environment, and the agent learns within that one environment, usually from a huge amount of trial and error.

With language agents, something new happens. Language models gave us the ability to *think*, to generate reasoning in language before acting. In my work on ReAct, the key insight was that thinking can be treated as a kind of action. It's a strange action, though. It doesn't change the external world. It changes the agent's own internal context. And the space of possible thoughts is essentially infinite. In traditional reinforcement learning that would be a nightmare, because you can't explore an infinite action space. But because language models come with strong priors from pretraining, the agent can actually use that infinite space well.

That's why I'd say the difference isn't just "we swapped in a bigger model." Traditional agents learn a policy *for* an environment. Language agents bring general priors and reasoning *to* an environment. That's where generalization comes from. A traditional agent trained on one game usually can't play another. A language agent can read the instructions, reason about the situation, and try something sensible the first time.

So I'd put it this way: traditional agents are defined by their environment, while language agents are defined by their ability to reason, and reasoning is what lets them transfer across environments. Of course, this raises new problems. How do you give them memory, how do they learn from experience, and how do you evaluate them in the real world? I think those are the interesting questions now.

r001.rationale: The response calls reasoning the most essential difference between language agents and traditional AI agents.

r002.rationale: It states that reasoning is what lets language agents transfer across environments.

r003.rationale: It says language models enable reasoning and that their strong priors from pretraining let agents use the otherwise infinite space of possible thoughts effectively.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the essential difference comes down to what the agent is built out of, and what that lets it do.

Traditional agents, the kind we studied in classic AI and in reinforcement learning, are defined by a very narrow interface. The state is a vector, the action is an index or a continuous control, and everything the agent "knows" has to be learned from scratch through reward in that specific environment. Atari, Go, robotics, these are the canonical examples. The agent is extremely good at one thing, but it has no priors about the world, no notion of concepts, and it can't carry anything over to a new task.

A language agent is different in a fundamental way: language is both the interface and the internal medium of thought. The actions the agent takes are text, the observations it gets back are text, and, most importantly, the reasoning happening in between is also text. That last part is what I find most interesting. When we did ReAct, the key idea was simply to let the model interleave thinking and acting, and that small change gave you things traditional agents never had, like the ability to decompose a task, notice an error, and adjust the plan, all in natural language, without any task-specific training.

So the way I'd put it is: traditional agents learn to act in a world; language agents come with a world model already built in, from pretraining on human text, and then act on top of it. That gives you generality and transfer almost for free. The flip side is that the environments are now open-ended, like the internet, code, or software, and that creates a whole new set of problems around how you evaluate them and how you make them reliable. That's really why I became interested in building benchmarks like WebShop and SWE-bench, because the old evaluation paradigm doesn't fit this new kind of agent.

r001.rationale: The response presents language agents’ ability to think in text and interleave reasoning with action as a fundamental difference from traditional agents.

r002.rationale: It says language agents gain “generality and transfer” from a pretrained world model, contrasting this with traditional agents’ inability to carry learning to new tasks.

r003.rationale: It mentions a world model built from pretraining, but does not clearly attribute language agents’ capacity to reason to a sufficiently strong prior supplied by language models.

astra-6.text:
I think the essential difference is the role language plays. In a traditional AI agent, you typically define a particular environment, an action space, and a reward function. The agent learns to map observations to actions within that setup. Language might be an input, but it isn’t necessarily the medium through which the agent reasons and acts.

For a language agent, language becomes a kind of general-purpose interface. The agent can describe what it observes, reason about what to do, use tools, and incorporate feedback—all through language, or structures closely connected to language. That makes it possible to take knowledge learned from text and apply it to tasks beyond the environment where the agent was trained.

But I wouldn’t draw the boundary simply at whether an agent uses a language model. The important thing is closing the loop between reasoning and action. It doesn’t just generate an answer; it takes an action, observes what actually happened, and updates its plan. Language gives us a flexible way to organize that loop, although it doesn’t automatically make the agent reliable.

r001.rationale: The response names language’s role as the essential difference. It says language agents can reason, but does not identify reasoning capacity itself as the essential difference.

r002.rationale: It says language agents can apply knowledge learned from text to tasks beyond the environment where they were trained, communicating generalization across environments.

r003.rationale: The response does not attribute language agents’ reasoning ability to a sufficiently strong prior supplied by language models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the essential difference is the role language plays in the system. In a traditional AI agent, you usually define an environment, an action space, and a reward function. The agent learns a policy within that setup. A language agent uses language as a more general interface for understanding tasks, reasoning about what to do, and interacting with its environment.

For example, it can take a goal expressed in natural language, break it into steps, use tools, observe the results, and revise its plan. Its actions might include writing code, searching for information, or asking someone a question. So the action space can be much more flexible than a fixed set of moves.

But I wouldn’t say they’re fundamentally separate concepts. A language agent is still an agent: it observes, acts, and receives feedback. What changes is that a language model brings prior knowledge and a flexible representation into that loop. That makes it easier to specify new tasks, while leaving the central challenge of agency—acting reliably over many steps—very much open.

r001.rationale: The response identifies language’s role as the essential difference and mentions reasoning as part of its interface, but does not identify the capacity to reason itself as the essential difference.

r002.rationale: It says language makes it easier to specify new tasks, but does not state that reasoning enables generalization across environments.

r003.rationale: It says language models bring prior knowledge, but does not attribute language agents’ ability to reason to that prior.
